pathways.name: Glycolysis: Investment
pathways.blurb: From glucose to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. The cell spends 2 ATP to prime the sugar.

nodes.i: Six-carbon sugar that enters cells through GLUT transporters. Glycolysis begins by trapping it inside the cell.
nodes.h: The six-carbon fuel sugar that starts the pathway.

nodes.i: Transfers a phosphate from ATP to glucose (glucokinase does this in liver and pancreatic beta cells). Inhibited by its own product.
nodes.h: Uses ATP to phosphorylate glucose. The liver version is called glucokinase.

nodes.i: Phosphorylated glucose that cannot leave the cell. It is also a branch point to glycogen synthesis and the pentose phosphate pathway.
nodes.h: First phosphorylated intermediate, and the branch point to the pentose phosphate pathway.

nodes.i: Converts an aldose (glucose-6-phosphate) to a ketose (fructose-6-phosphate) in a freely reversible reaction.
nodes.h: An isomerase that turns an aldose sugar phosphate into a ketose.

nodes.i: Ketose sugar phosphate that receives a second phosphate in the committed step.
nodes.h: Ketose sugar phosphate made by isomerisation, about to be phosphorylated again.

nodes.i: The rate-limiting, committed step. Activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate; inhibited by ATP and citrate.
nodes.h: Rate-limiting enzyme. ATP and citrate inhibit it, AMP activates it.

nodes.i: Six-carbon sugar carrying two phosphates, ready to be split into two three-carbon pieces. It also feeds forward to activate pyruvate kinase.
nodes.h: Six-carbon sugar carrying two phosphates, about to be cleaved.

nodes.i: Cleaves the six-carbon sugar into DHAP and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate. Aldolase B in the liver also handles fructose metabolism.
nodes.h: Cleaves a six-carbon sugar into two trioses.

nodes.i: Three-carbon triose that carries on down glycolysis. DHAP is converted into it by triose phosphate isomerase, so each glucose gives two.
nodes.h: The triose that proceeds onward. DHAP is converted into it by triose phosphate isomerase.

pathways.name: Glycolysis: Payoff
pathways.blurb: From glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate to pyruvate. NADH and 4 ATP are made per glucose.

nodes.i: Start of the payoff phase. Two molecules arrive per glucose.
nodes.h: Three-carbon triose. Two of them arrive per glucose.

nodes.i: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase. Oxidises the triose and adds inorganic phosphate, making NADH and a high-energy acyl phosphate.
nodes.h: Makes the first NADH of glycolysis. It adds inorganic phosphate, not ATP.

nodes.i: High-energy acyl phosphate that can donate a phosphate straight to ADP.
nodes.h: High-energy intermediate that hands its phosphate to ADP.

nodes.i: First substrate-level phosphorylation: makes ATP from ADP. Arsenate poisoning bypasses this step.
nodes.h: Makes the first ATP of the payoff phase by substrate-level phosphorylation.

nodes.i: Three-carbon acid with the phosphate on carbon 3. Also a precursor for serine synthesis.
nodes.h: Three-carbon acid with one phosphate on carbon 3. Precursor of serine.

nodes.i: Shifts the phosphate from carbon 3 to carbon 2.
nodes.h: Moves a phosphate from carbon 3 to carbon 2.

nodes.i: Phosphate now sits on carbon 2, setting up the loss of water.
nodes.h: Phosphate sits on carbon 2. It is about to lose water.

nodes.i: Removes water to create PEP. Inhibited by fluoride, which is why blood glucose tubes contain sodium fluoride.
Carries the highest-energy phosphate in glycolysis. Also an intermediate in gluconeogenesis.
nodes.h: Holds the highest-energy phosphate in glycolysis.

nodes.i: Second substrate-level phosphorylation and an irreversible step. Activated by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. Deficiency causes haemolytic anaemia.
nodes.h: Irreversible last enzyme. Its deficiency causes haemolytic anaemia.

nodes.i: End product of glycolysis. It becomes lactate (anaerobic), acetyl-CoA (aerobic), oxaloacetate or alanine.
nodes.h: Three-carbon end product that can become lactate or acetyl-CoA.

pathways.name: Citric Acid Cycle
pathways.blurb: Eight enzymes oxidise acetyl-CoA in the mitochondrial matrix. Read from oxaloacetate round to malate.

nodes.i: Four-carbon acceptor that combines with acetyl-CoA. It is regenerated at the end of every turn.
nodes.h: Four-carbon acid that picks up acetyl-CoA. Regenerated at the end of the cycle.

nodes.i: Condenses acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate to make citrate. Inhibited by ATP, NADH and succinyl-CoA.
nodes.h: The condensing enzyme that joins acetyl-CoA to a four-carbon acid.

nodes.i: First six-carbon product, and the molecule the cycle is named after. Also exported to the cytosol for fatty acid synthesis.
nodes.h: First six-carbon product. The cycle is named after it.

nodes.i: Iron-sulfur enzyme that isomerises citrate to isocitrate through cis-aconitate. Blocked by fluorocitrate.
nodes.h: Iron-sulfur enzyme that isomerises citrate. Fluoroacetate poisoning blocks it.

nodes.i: Isomer of citrate with the hydroxyl moved into position for oxidation.
nodes.h: Isomer of the first six-carbon product.

nodes.i: Rate-limiting step: releases the first CO2 and makes the first NADH. Activated by ADP and Ca2+, inhibited by ATP and NADH.
nodes.h: Rate-limiting enzyme. Releases the first CO2 and makes NADH.

nodes.i: Five-carbon keto acid. Accepts an amino group to become glutamate, linking the cycle to amino acid metabolism.
nodes.h: Five-carbon keto acid that becomes glutamate when it accepts an amino group.

nodes.i: Multi-enzyme complex that needs the same five cofactors as pyruvate dehydrogenase. Releases the second CO2 and makes NADH.
nodes.h: A complex using the same five cofactors as pyruvate dehydrogenase. Second CO2 leaves here.

nodes.i: High-energy thioester. Also the starting material for heme synthesis.
nodes.h: High-energy thioester that also feeds heme synthesis.

nodes.i: The cycle's substrate-level phosphorylation: makes GTP (or ATP) directly.
Four-carbon dicarboxylate released after the GTP step.
nodes.h: Four-carbon acid released after the GTP-forming step.

nodes.i: Also Complex II of the electron transport chain, and the only cycle enzyme embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Makes FADH2.
nodes.h: Membrane-bound enzyme that doubles as Complex II. Makes FADH2.

nodes.i: Four-carbon acid with a trans double bond. Also released as a by-product of the urea cycle.
nodes.h: Four-carbon acid with a double bond. Also a by-product of the urea cycle.

nodes.i: Adds water across the double bond of fumarate to give malate.
Hydroxyl-bearing four-carbon acid. Malate dehydrogenase oxidises it to oxaloacetate, makes the third NADH and closes the cycle.
nodes.h: The last intermediate. Oxidising it regenerates oxaloacetate.

pathways.name: Urea Cycle
pathways.blurb: How the liver turns toxic ammonia into urea. Starts in the mitochondria and finishes in the cytosol.

nodes.i: Toxic ammonia from amino acid breakdown joins bicarbonate inside liver mitochondria.
nodes.h: Toxic waste from amino acid breakdown, joined with bicarbonate in liver mitochondria.

nodes.i: Mitochondrial rate-limiting enzyme. Uses 2 ATP and needs N-acetylglutamate as an activator.
High-energy molecule that donates its carbamoyl group to ornithine.
nodes.h: High-energy donor of a carbamoyl group.

nodes.i: Combines carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine. X-linked deficiency causes hyperammonaemia with raised urinary orotic acid.
nodes.h: X-linked deficiency raises orotic acid in the urine.

nodes.i: Made inside the mitochondria and then exported to the cytosol.
nodes.h: Product of the mitochondrial step, exported to the cytosol.

nodes.i: Cytosolic enzyme that links citrulline to aspartate using ATP. Aspartate provides the second nitrogen of urea.
nodes.h: Cytosolic. Uses aspartate and ATP to supply the second nitrogen.

nodes.i: Intermediate formed from citrulline and aspartate.
nodes.h: Intermediate built from citrulline plus aspartate.

nodes.i: Cleaves argininosuccinate and releases fumarate, which links the urea cycle to the citric acid cycle.
nodes.h: Releases fumarate, linking this cycle to the citric acid cycle.

nodes.i: Substrate for the last step. Also the precursor of nitric oxide.
nodes.h: Substrate for the final step. Also makes nitric oxide.

nodes.i: Hydrolyses arginine to urea and ornithine. Ornithine returns to the mitochondria. Found mainly in the liver.
nodes.h: Splits arginine into urea and ornithine.

nodes.i: Water-soluble end product that travels in blood to the kidneys and leaves in urine.
nodes.h: Water-soluble nitrogen waste excreted by the kidneys.

pathways.name: Heme to Bilirubin
pathways.blurb: What happens to haemoglobin when old red cells die, from heme to the pigment in stool.

nodes.i: Released from haemoglobin when macrophages in the spleen and liver break down red cells at about 120 days.
nodes.h: Released from haemoglobin when old red cells are destroyed.

nodes.i: Opens the heme ring using O2 and NADPH, releasing iron and carbon monoxide. The only endogenous source of CO.
nodes.h: Opens the heme ring and releases iron and carbon monoxide.

nodes.i: Green pigment. It is the colour you see in a healing bruise.
nodes.h: Green pigment seen in a healing bruise.

nodes.i: Uses NADPH to reduce biliverdin to bilirubin.
nodes.h: Reduces the green pigment to a yellow one using NADPH.

nodes.i: Lipid-soluble and toxic, so it travels bound to albumin. It is not excreted in urine. Also called indirect bilirubin.
nodes.h: Lipid-soluble form carried on albumin. Not found in urine.

nodes.i: UGT1A1 in the hepatocyte smooth ER adds glucuronic acid. Reduced in Gilbert syndrome, absent in severe Crigler-Najjar.
nodes.h: Liver enzyme deficient in Gilbert and Crigler-Najjar syndromes.

nodes.i: Water-soluble (direct) bilirubin that is secreted into bile. Dubin-Johnson syndrome affects its secretion.
nodes.h: Water-soluble form that is secreted into bile.

nodes.i: Deconjugate and reduce bilirubin in the terminal ileum and colon.
nodes.h: Enzymes from intestinal flora that deconjugate and reduce bilirubin.

nodes.i: Colourless. Most is lost in faeces, some is reabsorbed into the enterohepatic circulation and a little reaches urine.
nodes.h: Colourless product. A little is reabsorbed and reaches the urine.

nodes.i: Brown pigment that colours stool. Stools turn pale when bile flow is obstructed.
nodes.h: Brown pigment of stool. Absent in obstructive jaundice.

pathways.name: Coagulation Cascade
pathways.blurb: Intrinsic pathway into the common pathway, from damaged vessel wall to a stable fibrin clot.

nodes.i: Vessel injury exposes subendothelial collagen, which activates factor XII and platelets.
nodes.h: Damage to the vessel wall exposes this structural protein.

nodes.i: Activated on negatively charged surfaces. Starts the intrinsic pathway.
nodes.h: The contact factor that starts the intrinsic pathway.

nodes.i: Activated by XIIa. Its deficiency (haemophilia C) causes mild bleeding.
nodes.h: Activated by XIIa and goes on to activate IX.

nodes.i: Works with factor VIIIa, calcium and phospholipid to activate X. Deficiency causes haemophilia B.
Start of the common pathway. With factor Va it forms prothrombinase. Blocked directly by rivaroxaban and apixaban.
nodes.h: Start of the common pathway. Blocked by rivaroxaban and apixaban.

nodes.i: Vitamin K-dependent precursor made in the liver (factors II, VII, IX and X all need vitamin K).
nodes.h: Vitamin K-dependent precursor made in the liver.

nodes.i: Master enzyme: cleaves fibrinogen and activates V, VIII, XI, XIII and platelets. Inhibited by antithrombin and dabigatran.
nodes.h: Cleaves fibrinogen and also activates factors V, VIII, XI and XIII.

nodes.i: Soluble plasma protein (factor I) made in the liver.
nodes.h: Soluble plasma protein made by the liver.

nodes.i: Formed when thrombin removes fibrinopeptides from fibrinogen. They self-assemble into a loose mesh.
nodes.h: Insoluble units that self-assemble into a loose mesh.

nodes.i: A transglutaminase activated by thrombin. Forms covalent cross-links between fibrin strands.
Cross-linked mesh that traps platelets and red cells. Later broken down by plasmin, releasing D-dimers.
nodes.h: Cross-linked mesh later broken down by plasmin.

pathways.name: Cardiac Conduction
pathways.blurb: The path of the electrical impulse from the heart's pacemaker to the ventricular muscle.

nodes.i: Sinoatrial node in the upper right atrium near the SVC opening. The natural pacemaker, firing at about 60 to 100 bpm.
nodes.h: The natural pacemaker, in the upper right atrium near the SVC.

nodes.i: Impulse spreads across both atria, causing atrial contraction (P wave).
nodes.h: Spread of the impulse across both atria produces the P wave.

nodes.i: Lies in the septum near the coronary sinus. Conducts slowly, which creates the PR interval and lets the ventricles fill.
nodes.h: Conducts slowly, giving the delay that lets the ventricles fill.

nodes.i: The only electrical bridge across the fibrous skeleton between atria and ventricles.
nodes.h: The only electrical bridge between atria and ventricles.

nodes.i: Right and left branches run down either side of the interventricular septum. The left divides into anterior and posterior fascicles.
nodes.h: Right and left branches running down the septum.

nodes.i: Large, fast-conducting fibres that spread the impulse through the subendocardium of both ventricles.
nodes.h: Fast fibres that spread the impulse through the ventricles.

nodes.i: Depolarises from endocardium to epicardium, producing the QRS complex and the ventricular contraction.
nodes.h: Its depolarisation produces the QRS complex.

pathways.name: Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone
pathways.blurb: How the kidney, lungs and adrenal cortex work together to raise a falling blood pressure.

nodes.i: Low blood pressure, low sodium at the macula densa or sympathetic activity stimulates juxtaglomerular cells.
nodes.h: Falling pressure in the kidney starts the cascade.

nodes.i: Inactive plasma protein made by the liver. Always available as renin's substrate.
nodes.h: Inactive plasma protein from the liver.

nodes.i: Protease released by juxtaglomerular cells. The rate-limiting step. Aliskiren inhibits it.
nodes.h: Released by juxtaglomerular cells. Rate-limiting step.

nodes.i: Inactive decapeptide cleaved from angiotensinogen.
Angiotensin-converting enzyme, mostly on lung endothelium. Also breaks down bradykinin, which explains the ACE-inhibitor cough.
nodes.h: Found on lung endothelium. Its inhibitors cause a dry cough.

nodes.i: Potent vasoconstrictor (AT1 receptor). Stimulates aldosterone, ADH and thirst, and constricts the efferent arteriole. Blocked by ARBs.
Steroid from the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex. Increases Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion in principal cells.
nodes.h: Steroid hormone from the zona glomerulosa.

nodes.i: Raises blood volume and pressure, which switches renin release off again by negative feedback.
nodes.h: Raises blood volume and so switches renin off.

pathways.name: Blood Flow Through the Heart
pathways.blurb: Follow a drop of blood from the body, through the lungs and back out to the aorta.

nodes.i: Superior and inferior vena cava return deoxygenated blood from the body.
nodes.h: Large veins returning deoxygenated blood from the body.

nodes.i: Receives blood from the vena cavae and the coronary sinus. Contains the SA node.
Three-leaflet valve with chordae tendineae and papillary muscles.
nodes.h: Three leaflets. Sits between right atrium and right ventricle.

nodes.i: Thin-walled chamber that pumps against the low-pressure pulmonary circuit.
nodes.h: Pumps against the low-pressure pulmonary circuit.

nodes.i: Semilunar valve at the right ventricular outflow.
nodes.h: Semilunar valve leaving the right ventricle.

nodes.i: The only arteries that carry deoxygenated blood.
nodes.h: The only arteries carrying deoxygenated blood.

nodes.i: Gas exchange at the alveolar capillaries: CO2 out, O2 in.
Four veins carrying oxygenated blood. The only veins to do so.
nodes.h: The only veins carrying oxygenated blood.

nodes.i: Receives the pulmonary veins. Its appendage is a common site for clot formation in atrial fibrillation.
Bicuspid valve between left atrium and left ventricle.
nodes.h: Two-leaflet valve between left atrium and left ventricle.

nodes.i: Thick-walled chamber generating systemic pressure. Perfused mainly during diastole.
nodes.h: Thickest-walled chamber, pumping to the whole body.

nodes.i: Semilunar valve. The coronary arteries arise just above it.
nodes.h: Semilunar valve. Coronary arteries arise just above it.

nodes.i: Largest artery. Its elastic recoil keeps blood moving during diastole.
nodes.h: Largest artery. Elastic recoil sustains diastolic pressure.

pathways.name: Gluconeogenesis
pathways.blurb: Making glucose from pyruvate in fasting. Four enzymes bypass the irreversible steps of glycolysis.

nodes.i: Made from lactate or alanine. Gluconeogenesis starts in the mitochondria.
nodes.h: Three-carbon starting point, made from lactate or alanine.

nodes.i: Mitochondrial. Needs biotin and ATP, and is activated by acetyl-CoA.
nodes.h: Biotin-dependent mitochondrial enzyme activated by acetyl-CoA.

nodes.i: Cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane, so it leaves as malate.
nodes.h: Four-carbon acid that leaves the mitochondria as malate.

nodes.i: Cytosolic. Uses GTP to convert oxaloacetate to PEP. Induced by glucagon and cortisol.
nodes.h: Uses GTP to convert oxaloacetate to PEP.

nodes.i: From here the pathway runs backwards through the reversible glycolytic steps.
nodes.h: High-energy phosphate compound. The pathway now runs backwards.

nodes.i: Enolase, phosphoglycerate mutase, phosphoglycerate kinase, GAPDH and aldolase all work in reverse.
nodes.h: A group of glycolytic enzymes that work in both directions.

nodes.i: Substrate of the second bypass enzyme.
nodes.h: Six-carbon sugar with two phosphates, about to lose one.

nodes.i: Rate-limiting step. Inhibited by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, activated by citrate.
nodes.h: Rate-limiting enzyme, the opposite of PFK-1.

nodes.i: Converted back to glucose-6-phosphate by the same isomerase used in glycolysis.
nodes.h: Ketose sugar phosphate, one step from glucose-6-phosphate.

nodes.i: Freely reversible, so it serves both glycolysis and gluconeogenesis.
nodes.h: Freely reversible isomerase shared with glycolysis.

nodes.i: Trapped inside the cell until it is dephosphorylated.
nodes.h: Phosphorylated glucose awaiting its final bypass enzyme.

nodes.i: In the ER of liver, kidney and intestine, and absent from muscle. Deficiency is von Gierke disease.
nodes.h: Absent in muscle. Deficiency causes von Gierke disease (GSD I).

nodes.i: Released into the blood to maintain fasting glucose.
nodes.h: The final product, released into the blood.

pathways.name: Glycogenolysis
pathways.blurb: Breaking liver glycogen down to free glucose between meals.

nodes.i: Branched glucose polymer stored in liver and muscle. A debranching enzyme handles the alpha-1,6 branch points.
nodes.h: Branched glucose polymer stored in liver and muscle.

nodes.i: Rate-limiting. Needs pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6). Cleaves alpha-1,4 bonds. Activated by glucagon, adrenaline and Ca2+.
nodes.h: Rate-limiting and needs vitamin B6. Cleaves alpha-1,4 bonds.

nodes.i: Released by phosphorolysis, so no ATP is spent at this step.
nodes.h: Released from chain ends without spending ATP.

nodes.i: Moves the phosphate from carbon 1 to carbon 6.
nodes.h: Moves a phosphate from carbon 1 to carbon 6.

nodes.i: Branch point between glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway and free glucose.
Liver only, so only liver glycogen can raise blood glucose. Muscle glycogen is used locally.
nodes.h: Liver enzyme that is missing from muscle.

nodes.i: Free glucose released into the blood by the liver.
nodes.h: Free sugar exported by the liver.

pathways.name: Glycogenesis
pathways.blurb: Building glycogen from glucose after a meal, driven by insulin.

nodes.i: Made from glucose by hexokinase or glucokinase.
Moves the phosphate from carbon 6 to carbon 1.
nodes.h: Moves a phosphate from carbon 6 to carbon 1.

nodes.i: Ready to be activated with UTP.
Uses UTP to activate glucose-1-phosphate. Pyrophosphate is then hydrolysed, making the step irreversible.
The activated glucose donor for glycogen synthase.
Rate-limiting. Adds glucose to alpha-1,4 chains on a glycogenin primer. Activated by insulin, inactivated by phosphorylation.
nodes.h: Rate-limiting enzyme that extends alpha-1,4 chains.

nodes.i: Long alpha-1,4 chain with no branches yet.
Moves a block of about 7 residues to create an alpha-1,6 branch, which makes glycogen soluble and quick to mobilise.
Many chain ends allow rapid release of glucose.

pathways.name: Pentose Phosphate Pathway
pathways.blurb: The oxidative phase that makes NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate.

nodes.i: Enters the pentose phosphate pathway in the cytosol.
nodes.h: Phosphorylated glucose that enters from glycolysis.

nodes.i: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase. Rate-limiting; makes the first NADPH. Deficiency causes haemolysis with fava beans, primaquine or infection.
nodes.h: Rate-limiting. Deficiency causes haemolysis after fava beans.

nodes.i: Unstable lactone intermediate.
Hydrolyses the lactone ring.
Acid substrate for the second oxidation.
Makes the second NADPH and releases CO2.
nodes.h: Makes the second NADPH and releases CO2.

nodes.i: Branch point: isomerised to ribose-5-phosphate, or converted to xylulose-5-phosphate for the non-oxidative phase.
nodes.h: Five-carbon ketose at the branch point.

nodes.i: Converts the ketose to an aldose.
Used to build nucleotides and nucleic acids.

pathways.name: Fructose Metabolism
pathways.blurb: How the liver handles fructose and feeds it into glycolysis, bypassing PFK-1.

nodes.i: From fruit, honey and sucrose.
nodes.h: Fruit sugar, from sucrose and honey.

nodes.i: Liver enzyme that traps fructose as fructose-1-phosphate. Deficiency causes benign essential fructosuria.
nodes.h: Liver kinase. Deficiency is benign (essential fructosuria).

nodes.i: Bypasses the main regulatory step of glycolysis.
Splits fructose-1-phosphate. Deficiency causes hereditary fructose intolerance with hypoglycaemia and liver injury.
Triose that still needs a phosphate.
Phosphorylates glyceraldehyde using ATP.
Joins the glycolytic pathway.

pathways.name: Galactose Metabolism
pathways.blurb: How milk sugar is converted to glucose derivatives.

nodes.i: From lactose in milk.
Phosphorylates galactose. Deficiency causes cataracts because galactitol builds up.
nodes.h: Deficiency causes cataracts but is otherwise mild.

nodes.i: Toxic if it accumulates.
Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase. Deficiency causes classic galactosaemia: jaundice, hepatomegaly, cataracts and E. coli sepsis.
Formed by exchanging the UDP carrier from glucose.
Flips carbon 4 to convert galactose back to glucose form.
Can enter glycogen synthesis or glycolysis.
nodes.h: The glucose form of the carrier.

pathways.name: Beta-Oxidation
pathways.blurb: Fatty acids to acetyl-CoA in the mitochondria, including the carnitine shuttle.

nodes.i: Mobilised from fat by hormone-sensitive lipase and carried on albumin.
nodes.h: Released from adipose and carried on albumin.

nodes.i: On the outer mitochondrial membrane. Uses ATP, costing two high-energy bonds, to activate the fatty acid.
nodes.h: Activates the fatty acid and costs the equivalent of 2 ATP.

nodes.i: Cannot cross the inner membrane without carnitine.
nodes.h: Activated fatty acid that needs carnitine.

nodes.i: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I. Rate-limiting and inhibited by malonyl-CoA.
Carried across the inner membrane by a translocase.
Matrix enzyme that regenerates acyl-CoA from acyl-carnitine.
nodes.h: Matrix side enzyme that releases carnitine.

nodes.i: Ready for the four-step beta-oxidation spiral.
nodes.h: Now inside the matrix and ready for oxidation.

nodes.i: First step. Makes FADH2. MCAD deficiency causes hypoketotic hypoglycaemia during fasting in children.
nodes.h: Makes FADH2. MCAD deficiency causes fasting hypoglycaemia.

nodes.i: Has a double bond between carbons 2 and 3.
Adds water across the double bond.
Has a hydroxyl on carbon 3.
Oxidises the hydroxyl and makes NADH.
Ready to be cleaved.
Cleaves off acetyl-CoA, leaving an acyl-CoA two carbons shorter.
nodes.h: Cleaves off two carbons as acetyl-CoA.

nodes.i: Enters the citric acid cycle or, in the liver, ketogenesis.
nodes.h: Two-carbon product that enters the citric acid cycle.

pathways.name: Fatty Acid Synthesis
pathways.blurb: From mitochondrial acetyl-CoA to palmitate in the cytosol, fed by insulin.

nodes.i: Cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane.
nodes.h: Two-carbon unit trapped in the mitochondria.

nodes.i: Exported when ATP and citrate are high. Citrate also activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase.
nodes.h: Six-carbon carrier that exports acetyl units.

nodes.i: Regenerates cytosolic acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate. Activated by insulin.
Substrate for the committed step.
Rate-limiting. Needs biotin and ATP. Activated by insulin and citrate, inhibited by glucagon, AMPK and palmitoyl-CoA.
Also inhibits CPT-I, so synthesis and oxidation do not run together.
Multi-enzyme complex that uses NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway.
The 16-carbon product. Elongation and desaturation occur in the ER.

pathways.name: Ketogenesis
pathways.blurb: How the liver makes ketone bodies during fasting and in diabetic ketoacidosis.

nodes.i: Builds up in the liver in fasting because oxaloacetate is diverted to gluconeogenesis.
Joins two acetyl-CoA molecules.
Four-carbon thioester.
Rate-limiting step of ketogenesis. This is the mitochondrial isoform.
Also an intermediate in cholesterol synthesis, in the cytosol.
nodes.h: Six-carbon intermediate shared with cholesterol synthesis.

nodes.i: Cleaves HMG-CoA into acetoacetate and acetyl-CoA.
First ketone body. It spontaneously makes acetone, the fruity breath of ketoacidosis.
nodes.h: First ketone body; can break down to acetone.

nodes.i: Uses NADH to reduce acetoacetate.
The main ketone in blood, and the one missed by nitroprusside urine tests. The liver cannot use ketones.
nodes.h: Main blood ketone, missed by urine dipsticks.

pathways.name: Cholesterol Synthesis
pathways.blurb: From acetyl-CoA to cholesterol in the cytosol and ER. The statin target is the rate-limiting step.

nodes.i: Starting unit for all steroids.
Cytosolic isoform, unlike the mitochondrial one used for ketones.
Six-carbon intermediate.
Rate-limiting. Inhibited by statins and by cholesterol, activated by insulin and thyroid hormone.
Six-carbon acid formed using NADPH.
Phosphorylations and a decarboxylation, using ATP.
Five-carbon isoprene building block.
Joins farnesyl pyrophosphate units.
nodes.h: Joins isoprene-derived units into a 30-carbon chain.

nodes.i: Thirty-carbon linear hydrocarbon.
Convert squalene into the four-ring steroid skeleton.
First sterol product.
About 19 steps that remove methyl groups and reduce double bonds.
nodes.h: Trim methyl groups from the ring system.

nodes.i: Precursor of bile acids, steroid hormones and vitamin D, and a membrane component.
nodes.h: Final product and precursor of steroid hormones.

pathways.name: Purine Degradation
pathways.blurb: From adenosine to uric acid. The enzymes behind SCID and gout.

nodes.i: Formed from AMP breakdown.
Deficiency causes SCID because toxic dATP builds up in lymphocytes.
Deaminated adenosine.
Deficiency causes a T-cell immunodeficiency.
Free purine base. HGPRT can salvage it.
Inhibited by allopurinol and febuxostat.
Intermediate purine.
Converts xanthine to uric acid.
Poorly soluble end product in humans. Excess causes gout. HGPRT deficiency (Lesch-Nyhan) overproduces it.
nodes.h: Poorly soluble end product that crystallises in gout.

pathways.name: Heme Synthesis
pathways.blurb: Mitochondrial and cytosolic steps, and the porphyria linked to each enzyme.

nodes.i: Condense in the mitochondria. Succinyl-CoA comes from the citric acid cycle.
nodes.h: Two precursors that condense in the mitochondria.

nodes.i: Rate-limiting and needs vitamin B6. Inhibited by heme. Defective in X-linked sideroblastic anaemia.
nodes.h: Rate-limiting, needs vitamin B6, repressed by heme.

nodes.i: Exported to the cytosol.
Inhibited by lead.
Pyrrole ring.
Deficiency causes acute intermittent porphyria: abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric signs, port-wine urine.
Linear tetrapyrrole.
Closes the ring. Deficiency causes congenital erythropoietic porphyria.
nodes.h: Closes the ring to form the correct isomer.

nodes.i: Cyclic tetrapyrrole.
Deficiency causes porphyria cutanea tarda, the most common porphyria, with blistering skin.
Returns to the mitochondria.
Deficiency causes hereditary coproporphyria.
Substrate for oxidation.
Deficiency causes variegate porphyria.
Ready for iron insertion.
Inserts Fe2+. Inhibited by lead.
nodes.h: Inserts iron. Also inhibited by lead.

nodes.i: Used in haemoglobin, myoglobin and cytochromes.

pathways.name: Electron Transport Chain
pathways.blurb: Electrons from NADH to oxygen, building the proton gradient that drives ATP synthase.

nodes.i: From the citric acid cycle and beta-oxidation. Delivers electrons to Complex I.
NADH dehydrogenase. Pumps 4 H+. Blocked by rotenone.
Lipid-soluble carrier that also accepts electrons from Complex II.
Cytochrome bc1. Pumps 4 H+. Blocked by antimycin A.
nodes.h: Cytochrome bc1, blocked by antimycin A.
